craft_claim: Non-Anglophone traditions practise affiliative warmth (Japanese haibun companionship; Persian adab counsel; Southern African ubuntu humaneness), but what counts as warm differs, so no single technique is universal.

supporting_evidence.location: Oku no Hosomichi (1689 journey; Yuasa trans. 1966)
supporting_evidence.note: Basho's haibun records a long journey with a companion and addresses readers as fellow travellers, producing unhurried companionable warmth through ordinary places.
Sa'di offers moral counsel in an adab register of simple elegant prose, presenting severe instruction as a friend's advice sweetened with wit.
Ramose grounds humaneness in the maxim umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu (a person is a person through other persons), making affiliation an ontological rather than merely stylistic matter.

counterevidence.note: The claimed universality of positive politeness has been repeatedly contested in cross-cultural pragmatics (e.g., Japanese solidarity and honorific systems behave differently), so forms must not be exported as universals.

scope: Cross-cultural deployment of the tone; establishes function-level commonality while refusing technique-level universals.
exceptions: Cultures where unsolicited familiarity registers as intrusion rather than kindness.
